chapter_note.simple: Bayes' theorem lets you work backwards from what you see to what probably caused it. You start with a belief about each possible cause, then check how well each cause explains the evidence, and rescale so the beliefs add up to 1. A rare cause can stay unlikely even after good-looking evidence, because the many ordinary cases produce more false alarms than the few real ones. Trees, counting 10,000 people and odds are three ways to do the same sum. Think of a detective who updates every suspect each time a new clue arrives.

cards.title: Law of total probability
cards.idea: A factory has two machines. You pick one finished item and ask: what is the chance it is defective? It came from machine 1 or machine 2, so add 'machine 1 and defective' to 'machine 2 and defective'. That is the **law of total probability**: split into cases that do not overlap, then add each case's share.
cards.idea_full: A factory has two machines. You pick one finished item at random and ask: what is the chance it is defective? The item came from machine 1 or from machine 2, and nowhere else. So work out the chance of 'machine 1 and defective', then 'machine 2 and defective', and add them. That is the **law of total probability**: split everything into cases that do not overlap, then add each case's share.
cards.definition:
$$P(B)=\sum_i P(A_i)\,P(B\mid A_i)$$

Symbols: A_1, A_2, ... are the cases. They cover every possibility and never overlap, so their probabilities add to 1. The event B is what you care about. The bar in P(B | A_i) reads 'given', so it is the chance of B when case i is true.

Each product P(A_i) × P(B | A_i) is one route to B. The sum adds up all the routes.

example.setup: Machine 1 makes 60% of the items and 2% of its items are defective. Machine 2 makes 40% and 5% of its items are defective. One item is picked at random.
steps: The cases are M1 (probability 0.6) and M2 (probability 0.4). They add to 1.
example.answer: P(defective) = 0.032, which is 3.2%. A plain average of 2% and 5% would give 3.5%, which is wrong because machine 1 makes more items.

cards.why: You need P(B) whenever you know the chance of B inside each case but not overall. It is also the bottom line of Bayes' formula. In GATE: you are given P(T), P(S | T) and P(S | not T), and you must first find P(S) like this.
how: List cases that cover every possibility and do not overlap.
For each case, multiply its probability by P(B | case).
Add the products.
Sanity check: the answer must lie between the smallest and largest P(B | case). Here it lies between 0.02 and 0.05.
cards.mistake: Averaging the conditional probabilities without weights, for example (0.02 + 0.05) / 2 = 0.035. Machine 1 makes more items, so it must count for more. Weight each case by its share.

check.q: It rains on 20% of days. The bus is late with probability 0.4 on a rainy day and 0.1 on a dry day. What is P(late)?
check.a: Rain route: 0.2 × 0.4 = 0.08. Dry route: 0.8 × 0.1 = 0.08. Add: P(late) = 0.16.

check.q: A coin is fair with probability 0.7 and biased (P(heads) = 0.9) with probability 0.3. What is P(heads)?

cards.simple: Your cricket team plays half its matches on a dry pitch and half on a wet one. It wins 60% of the dry matches and 30% of the wet ones. To find the overall win rate, you take half of 60% and half of 30% and add them, which gives 45%. You cannot just average 60 and 30 if the two pitches are not equally common. Each situation counts as much as it happens. In exam words: the law of total probability, P(B) = sum of P(case) × P(B | case).
cards.intuition_full: Total probability is a weighted average. Each case has a weight, its own probability, and a value, the chance of B inside that case. The overall chance is the weighted average of the values. That is why the answer must land between the smallest and the largest conditional value, and it is why a plain average is wrong whenever the weights differ. Picture the sample space as a rectangle split into vertical strips, one per case. Each strip is as wide as its probability. Inside each strip, a shaded block of height P(B | case) marks B. The total shaded area is P(B): width times height, summed over strips. If you forget a case, you forget a strip, so the cases must cover everything and must not overlap.

cards.title: Bayes' formula, prior and posterior
cards.idea: Total probability goes from cause to effect. Bayes goes backward: you find a defective item and ask which machine made it. Your belief before looking is the **prior**, and your belief after is the **posterior**. The change depends on how likely each machine was to produce the evidence, the **likelihood**.
cards.idea_full: Total probability goes forward, from a cause to an effect. Bayes goes backward. You find a defective item and ask which machine most likely made it. Before looking, you had a belief about each machine, called the **prior**. The evidence changes that belief into a new one, the **posterior**. How much it changes depends on how likely each machine was to produce the evidence, called the **likelihood**.
cards.definition:
$$P(A\mid B)=\frac{P(A)\,P(B\mid A)}{P(B)}$$

Symbols: P(A) is the prior, your belief in A before seeing B. P(B | A) is the likelihood, the chance of seeing B if A is true. P(B) is the evidence, found by total probability: the sum of prior × likelihood over all cases. P(A | B) is the posterior, your belief in A after seeing B.

Watch the direction. P(B | A) and P(A | B) are different numbers.

example.setup: Same factory as the last card: machine 1 makes 60% (2% defective) and machine 2 makes 40% (5% defective). An item is found defective. What is the chance it came from machine 2?
steps: Likelihood of 'defective': 0.02 under M1 and 0.05 under M2.
Add them to get the evidence: P(defective) = 0.012 + 0.020 = 0.032.
example.answer: P(M2 | defective) = 0.625. The prior for M2 was 0.4. It rose because M2 makes more defective items per item. The same working gives P(M1 | defective) = 0.375.

cards.why: Real data arrives as effects, and we want the causes: a disease from a test, a class from its features. In GATE: a two-hypothesis posterior from three given numbers. In ML, the same formula powers naive Bayes classifiers.
how: Name the hypotheses (the possible causes).
For each, multiply its prior by the likelihood of what was observed.
Add those products. That is the denominator.
Divide the product you want by the total.
Check: the posteriors of all hypotheses add to 1.
cards.mistake: Reporting the likelihood as the posterior. Here P(defective | M2) = 0.05, but P(M2 | defective) = 0.625. They answer different questions. Always finish by dividing by the total.

check.a: False. They are equal only when P(A) = P(B).

cards.what_full:
Total probability goes forward, from a cause to an effect. Bayes goes backward. You find a defective item and ask which machine most likely made it. Before looking, you had a belief about each machine, called the **prior**. The evidence changes that belief into a new one, the **posterior**. How much it changes depends on how likely each machine was to produce the evidence, called the **likelihood**.

$$P(A\mid B)=\frac{P(A)\,P(B\mid A)}{P(B)}$$

Symbols: P(A) is the prior, your belief in A before seeing B. P(B | A) is the likelihood, the chance of seeing B if A is true. P(B) is the evidence, found by total probability: the sum of prior × likelihood over all cases. P(A | B) is the posterior, your belief in A after seeing B.

Watch the direction. P(B | A) and P(A | B) are different numbers.

**Worked example.** Same factory as the last card: machine 1 makes 60% (2% defective) and machine 2 makes 40% (5% defective). An item is found defective. What is the chance it came from machine 2?

1. Priors: P(M1) = 0.6 and P(M2) = 0.4.
2. Likelihood of 'defective': 0.02 under M1 and 0.05 under M2.
3. Multiply prior × likelihood. M1: 0.6 × 0.02 = 0.012. M2: 0.4 × 0.05 = 0.020.
4. Add them to get the evidence: P(defective) = 0.012 + 0.020 = 0.032.
5. Divide: P(M2 | defective) = 0.020 / 0.032 = 0.625.

**Answer:** P(M2 | defective) = 0.625. The prior for M2 was 0.4. It rose because M2 makes more defective items per item. The same working gives P(M1 | defective) = 0.375.

**Check yourself:** P(A) = 0.25, P(B | A) = 0.6 and P(B | not A) = 0.2. Find P(A | B).

*Answer:* A: 0.25 × 0.6 = 0.15. Not A: 0.75 × 0.2 = 0.15. Total = 0.30. P(A | B) = 0.15 / 0.30 = 0.5.
cards.trap: Reporting the likelihood as the posterior. Here P(defective | M2) = 0.05, but P(M2 | defective) = 0.625. They answer different questions. Always finish by dividing by the total.

cards.simple: Two factories make pens. Factory 2 makes fewer pens, but its pens leak more often. You pick a leaking pen from the mixed pile. Which factory made it? Start with how many pens each factory makes. Then weight each factory by how often its pens leak. Then rescale so the two chances add up to 1. A factory that makes few pens but leaks a lot can still be the best guess. In exam words: posterior = prior × likelihood, divided by the evidence.
cards.intuition_full: Bayes' formula answers the backward question. Total probability tells you how likely the evidence is overall, and Bayes tells you which cause is most responsible for it. Think of all the ways the evidence can happen. Each cause gives one way, with size prior × likelihood. The posterior of a cause is its share of all those ways. A cause with a large prior but a tiny likelihood gets a small share. A cause with a tiny prior but a huge likelihood can still win. The denominator exists only to rescale the shares so they add up to 1. That also explains why you can skip it when you only compare two causes: the ratio of the shares is the ratio of prior × likelihood.

examples.answer: P(T | S) = 0.28. The likelihood 0.7 is not the answer: it points in the other direction.

examples.setup: Same numbers, but now S is NOT observed. Find P(T | not S).
steps: The observed evidence is 'not S', so use its likelihoods: P(not S | T) = 1 - 0.7 = 0.3 and P(not S | not T) = 1 - 0.2 = 0.8.
examples.answer: P(T | not S) = 0.04. Using P(S | T) = 0.7 here would be the wrong-likelihood trap.

A prior of 0 or 1 never changes, whatever the evidence.
If the likelihood is the same under every cause, the posterior equals the prior.
Posteriors over all causes always add to 1.

cards.title: Tree diagrams
cards.idea: A probability tree keeps Bayes arithmetic tidy. Each fork is one step, such as which box, then which ball. Write the chance on every branch. Multiply along a path, and add paths that give the same outcome.
cards.idea_full: Bayes arithmetic is easy to lose track of. A probability tree keeps it tidy. Each fork is one step: first which box you pick, then which ball you draw. Write the chance on every branch. The chance of a whole path is the product of the branches on it. If the same outcome appears on several paths, add those paths.
cards.definition:
Rules for reading a tree.

1. The branches leaving any node add to 1.
2. **Multiply along** a path to get the chance of that whole path.
3. **Add across** paths when an outcome can happen in more than one way.
4. After you see evidence, keep only the paths that match it. The posterior is one path divided by the sum of the kept paths.

$$P(\text{Box1}\mid W)=\frac{P(\text{Box1})\,P(W\mid\text{Box1})}{\sum\text{ all white paths}}$$

Here W means 'a white ball was drawn'.

example.setup: Box 1 has 3 white and 1 black ball. Box 2 has 1 white and 3 black. A box is picked at random and one ball is drawn. It is white. What is the chance it came from Box 1?
steps: First fork: Box 1 and Box 2 each have probability 0.5.
Second fork. From Box 1: white 3/4 = 0.75, black 0.25. From Box 2: white 1/4 = 0.25, black 0.75.
We saw white, so the black paths did not happen. P(Box 1 | white) = 0.375 / (0.375 + 0.125) = 0.75.
example.answer: P(Box 1 | white) = 0.75. Along the way you also found P(white) = 0.375 + 0.125 = 0.5.

cards.why: A tree makes box and coin problems mechanical and stops you from missing a case. In GATE: box, ball and coin questions with one or more draws.
how: Draw the first choice and label its branches.
From each branch draw the second step and label it.
Multiply along each path.
Cross out paths that contradict the evidence.
Divide the path you want by the sum of the surviving paths.
cards.mistake: Adding along a path, or forgetting to cross out the paths that did not happen. Along a path you multiply. After the evidence, only matching paths remain, and the answer is a share of those.

cards.simple: A tree is a map of choices. First you choose a bag, and then you choose a sweet from it. Along each branch you write how likely that choice is. To get the chance of one whole route, multiply the numbers along it, like multiplying the odds of each step. If the same result can be reached by two routes, add the routes. When you learn what you saw, throw away the routes that do not match and compare the rest. In exam words: multiply along a path, add across paths, then divide by the total of the paths that match the evidence.
cards.intuition_full: A tree stores every possible story in order, so nothing gets lost. Each path is one complete story of what happened, and its probability is the product of the branches because each step is conditional on the earlier ones. All the paths together add to 1, which is a good check. When you observe something, some stories are impossible and drop out. The stories that remain keep their relative sizes, so you divide by their total to rescale. That is Bayes' theorem done with a picture instead of a formula. If a tree gets big, collapse branches that lead to the same outcome, but never collapse branches with different probabilities.

examples.setup: Box 1 has 3 white and 1 black ball. Box 2 has 1 white and 3 black. A box is picked at random and one ball is drawn. It is white. What is the chance it came from Box 1?
steps: First fork: Box 1 and Box 2 each have probability 0.5.
Second fork. From Box 1: white 3/4 = 0.75, black 0.25. From Box 2: white 1/4 = 0.25, black 0.75.
We saw white, so the black paths did not happen. P(Box 1 | white) = 0.375 / (0.375 + 0.125) = 0.75.
examples.answer: P(Box 1 | white) = 0.75. Along the way you also found P(white) = 0.375 + 0.125 = 0.5.

examples.setup: Box A has 2 red and 3 blue balls. Box B has 4 red and 1 blue. A box is chosen at random and one ball is drawn. It is blue. Find the probability that it came from box A.
steps: First fork: box A 1/2, box B 1/2.
Blue from A: 3/5. Blue from B: 1/5.
Path A then blue: 1/2 × 3/5 = 0.30. Path B then blue: 1/2 × 1/5 = 0.10.
Keep only the blue paths. P(A | blue) = 0.30 / (0.30 + 0.10) = 0.75.
examples.answer: P(A | blue) = 0.75. You also found P(blue) = 0.40 along the way.

examples.setup: Same boxes. Now two balls are drawn from the chosen box WITHOUT replacement, and both are red. Find P(box A | both red).
steps: Update the box after the first red. Box A: 2/5 then 1/4 = 1/10. Box B: 4/5 then 3/4 = 3/5.
With replacement (wrongly) you would get A: 4/25, B: 16/25, giving 1/5.
examples.answer: P(A | both red) = 1/7. The second branch must use the updated box contents.

A branch with probability 0 can be left out.
One piece of evidence may match several paths: add them.
If a path has two steps, its probability is the product, even if the second step depends on the first.

cards.title: Base-rate fallacy
cards.idea: Suppose a test catches 90% of sick people, and you test positive. You may still very likely be healthy. When a disease is rare, healthy people far outnumber sick ones, so a small false-alarm rate still makes a crowd of false positives. Ignoring how common the disease is, the **base rate**, is the **base-rate fallacy**.
cards.idea_full: Suppose a test catches 90% of sick people, and you test positive. Surprisingly, you may still very likely be healthy. The reason is how many healthy people there are. If a disease is rare, healthy people far outnumber sick ones, so even a small false-alarm rate produces a crowd of false positives. Ignoring how common the disease is, the **base rate**, is the **base-rate fallacy**.
cards.definition:
Sensitivity is P(positive | sick). The false-positive rate is P(positive | healthy). Specificity is P(negative | healthy), so false-positive rate = 1 - specificity. Prevalence, or base rate, is P(sick).

$$P(\text{sick}\mid +)=\frac{\text{prev}\times\text{sens}}{\text{prev}\times\text{sens}+(1-\text{prev})\times\text{FPR}}$$

Symbols: prev is the prevalence, sens is the sensitivity and FPR is the false-positive rate. The easiest way to use it is to imagine 10,000 people and count.

example.setup: 1 person in 200 has a disease. The test is positive for 90% of the sick and for 4% of the healthy. You test positive. How likely are you to be sick?
steps: Imagine 10,000 people. 1 in 200 is 50 sick, so 9,950 are healthy.
Sick people who test positive: 90% of 50 = 45.
Healthy people who test positive: 4% of 9,950 = 398.
Chance you are sick, given positive: 45 / 443, about 0.102.

cards.title: Sequential updating and normalising
cards.idea: A box holds a fair coin and a two-headed coin. You pick one blindly and toss it, and it lands heads. The two-headed coin now looks more likely, and a second heads makes it more likely again. Each toss is new evidence: multiply each belief by how likely that toss was, then rescale so the beliefs add to 1.

A second heads makes it look even more likely. Each toss is new evidence. Each time, multiply your current belief in each coin by how likely that toss was for that coin, then rescale so the beliefs add to 1.
cards.definition:
$$P(H_i\mid E)=\frac{P(H_i)\,P(E\mid H_i)}{\sum_j P(H_j)\,P(E\mid H_j)}$$

Symbols: H_i is hypothesis i, such as 'this is the fair coin'. E is the evidence, such as 'heads'. The short form is posterior ∝ prior × likelihood, where ∝ means 'proportional to'.

**Normalising** means dividing every product by their sum so the answers add to 1. Tosses are independent once you know which coin it is, so the likelihood of a whole sequence is the product of the single-toss likelihoods. You can update one toss at a time or all at once.

example.setup: A box has a fair coin and a two-headed coin, equally likely. One coin is picked and tossed twice. Both tosses are heads. What is the chance it is the two-headed coin?
steps: First heads. Fair: 0.5 × 0.5 = 0.25. Two-headed: 0.5 × 1 = 0.5. Total 0.75. Posterior: fair 1/3, two-headed 2/3.
Check all at once. Fair: 0.5 × 0.5 × 0.5 = 0.125. Two-headed: 0.5 × 1 × 1 = 0.5. Then 0.5 / 0.625 = 0.8. Same answer.

The likelihood of a whole sequence is the product of single-toss likelihoods only because the tosses are independent once the hypothesis is fixed. A hypothesis that predicts the data badly gets multiplied by a small number again and again, so its share collapses fast. A hypothesis with likelihood 0 for even one observation is eliminated for ever.

cards.intuition_full: In a noisy channel the hidden cause is the bit that was sent, and the evidence is what you received. The likelihood is the channel's behaviour: how often a sent 1 arrives as 1, how often a sent 0 arrives as 1. The recipe is the same as always. Multiply each prior by the likelihood of exactly what you saw. Add up all the products. Divide. With more than two hypotheses nothing changes except the length of the list. In the three-boxes version, each box is a hypothesis, each box has its own chance of giving a white ball, and you divide the box you care about by the sum over all three.

examples.setup: A bit is 1 with probability 0.4 and 0 with probability 0.6. The channel flips any bit with probability 0.1. A 1 is received. What is the chance a 1 was sent?
steps: Likelihood of receiving 1. If 1 was sent, no flip: 0.9. If 0 was sent, a flip: 0.1.
examples.answer: About 0.857. The received 1 is strong evidence because flips are rare.

examples.setup: Three boxes are chosen with probabilities 0.2, 0.3 and 0.5. A white ball is drawn with probabilities 0.6, 0.4 and 0.1 from boxes 1, 2, 3. A white ball is drawn. Find the probability it came from box 1.
examples.answer: 12/29, about 0.414. The box with the biggest prior (box 3) comes last, because its white probability is tiny.

examples.setup: A bit is 1 or 0 with equal probability. It is sent twice and each copy is flipped independently with probability 0.2. The received pair is 1, 0. Find the probability a 1 was sent.
steps: If 1 was sent, receiving 1 then 0 means no flip then a flip: 0.8 × 0.2 = 0.16.
If 0 was sent, receiving 1 then 0 means a flip then no flip: 0.2 × 0.8 = 0.16.
examples.answer: 0.5. The evidence is equally likely under both hypotheses, so it tells you nothing.

edge_cases: Equal likelihoods under all hypotheses leave the prior unchanged.
The evidence must be exactly what was observed, such as 'received 1' or 'item non-defective'.
With k hypotheses, k joints and one normalising sum.
If the channel is symmetric and priors are equal, the posterior is the likelihood ratio normalised.
connections: Error-correcting codes extend this to many bits.
Naive Bayes sums log-likelihoods over features.
Three hypotheses are the same as the card on total probability with three cases.

cards.title: Conditional independence
cards.idea: Two motion sensors guard a shop, and each is unreliable on its own. If you knew whether there was a burglary, one sensor would tell you nothing about the other. If you do not know, one sounding makes the other more likely, because both hint at a burglary. Independence that holds only after fixing the cause is **conditional independence**.
cards.idea_full: Two motion sensors guard a shop. Each sensor is unreliable, but each is unreliable by itself. If you already knew whether there was a burglary, one sensor would tell you nothing about the other. If you do not know, one sounding makes the other more likely to sound, because it hints at a burglary. Independence that holds only after you fix the cause is **conditional independence**.
cards.definition:
$$P(A\cap B\mid H)=P(A\mid H)\,P(B\mid H)$$

Symbols: A and B are two observations, such as 'sensor 1 sounds' and 'sensor 2 sounds'. H is the hidden cause. The formula says A and B are independent once H is known.

It does not say P(A and B) = P(A) × P(B). Without H, the two observations are linked through it. To get P(A and B), compute the product inside each case and then add the cases.

example.setup: A shop is burgled on 2% of nights. Given the state, the sensors work independently. Each sounds with probability 0.8 if there is a burglary and 0.05 if there is not. Both sound. What is the chance of a burglary?
steps: Both sound, given burglary: 0.8 × 0.8 = 0.64. Given no burglary: 0.05 × 0.05 = 0.0025.
example.answer: About 0.839. Note that P(one sensor sounds) = 0.02 × 0.8 + 0.98 × 0.05 = 0.065. If the sensors were independent without the cause, P(both) would be 0.065² = 0.004225, far below the true 0.01525.

cards.why: This assumption is the heart of naive Bayes classifiers: features are independent given the class. In GATE: repeated observations that share a hidden cause, such as several tosses of the same coin.
how: Find the hidden cause, the thing that links the observations.
Assume the observations are independent given each value of the cause.
Under each hypothesis, multiply the per-observation likelihoods.
Multiply by the priors and normalise.
Never multiply the unconditional probabilities of the observations.
cards.mistake: Computing P(both) as P(A) × P(B). The observations are linked through the cause. Fix the cause first, multiply inside each case, then add the cases.

$$P(A\cap B\mid H)=P(A\mid H)\,P(B\mid H)$$

Symbols: A and B are two observations, such as 'sensor 1 sounds' and 'sensor 2 sounds'. H is the hidden cause. The formula says A and B are independent once H is known.

It does not say P(A and B) = P(A) × P(B). Without H, the two observations are linked through it. To get P(A and B), compute the product inside each case and then add the cases.

**Worked example.** A shop is burgled on 2% of nights. Given the state, the sensors work independently. Each sounds with probability 0.8 if there is a burglary and 0.05 if there is not. Both sound. What is the chance of a burglary?

1. Priors: burglary 0.02, no burglary 0.98.
2. Both sound, given burglary: 0.8 × 0.8 = 0.64. Given no burglary: 0.05 × 0.05 = 0.0025.
3. Joints. Burglary: 0.02 × 0.64 = 0.0128. No burglary: 0.98 × 0.0025 = 0.00245.
4. Evidence: P(both sound) = 0.0128 + 0.00245 = 0.01525.
5. Posterior: 0.0128 / 0.01525, about 0.839.

**Answer:** About 0.839. Note that P(one sensor sounds) = 0.02 × 0.8 + 0.98 × 0.05 = 0.065. If the sensors were independent without the cause, P(both) would be 0.065² = 0.004225, far below the true 0.01525.

cards.simple: Two friends tell you it rained last night, and each of them is sometimes wrong. If it really rained, whether friend 1 says so has nothing to do with friend 2: they check separately. But if you do not know whether it rained, one friend saying yes makes the other friend more likely to say yes, because both are hinting at the same weather. The two answers are independent only once you fix the real weather. In exam words: conditional independence, independent given the hypothesis but not unconditionally.
cards.intuition_full: Two observations share a hidden cause. Once you know the cause, they have nothing else in common, so you may multiply their probabilities. Without the cause, they are linked: seeing one makes the cause more likely, and that makes the other more likely too. So the probability of both is not the product of the two unconditional probabilities. The correct way is to fix each possible cause, multiply inside that case, weight by the prior, and add over the cases. This is the idea behind naive Bayes classifiers, where features are assumed independent given the class, and it is also why repeated tosses of one unknown coin are independent only given the coin.

examples.setup: A shop is burgled on 2% of nights. Given the state, the sensors work independently. Each sounds with probability 0.8 if there is a burglary and 0.05 if there is not. Both sound. What is the chance of a burglary?
steps: Both sound, given burglary: 0.8 × 0.8 = 0.64. Given no burglary: 0.05 × 0.05 = 0.0025.
examples.answer: About 0.839. Note that P(one sensor sounds) = 0.02 × 0.8 + 0.98 × 0.05 = 0.065. If the sensors were independent without the cause, P(both) would be 0.065² = 0.004225, far below the true 0.01525.

examples.setup: A patient has the flu with probability 0.1. Given the state, fever and cough appear independently. With flu: fever 0.8 and cough 0.7. Without flu: fever 0.1 and cough 0.2. Both symptoms appear. Find P(flu).
examples.answer: 28/37, about 0.757. The multiplication of fever and cough probabilities is allowed only inside each case.

examples.setup: Same patient. Now fever appears but cough does not. Find P(flu). Also compare P(fever and cough) with P(fever) × P(cough).
steps: P(fever and cough) = 0.056 + 0.018 = 0.074, which is far above 0.0425.
So the symptoms are NOT independent without the flu.
examples.answer: P(flu) = 0.25. The two symptoms are linked through the flu: 0.074 against 0.0425.

edge_cases: Conditional independence does not imply unconditional independence, and the reverse is also false.
If the cause is known, add nothing: just multiply.
If an observation is absent, use 1 minus its probability inside each case.
A missing common cause (an unmodelled one) breaks the assumption.
connections: Naive Bayes in ML uses exactly this assumption.
Repeated coin tosses from an unknown coin are conditionally independent given the coin (card b6).
Independence in prob.axioms is the unconditional version.

scenes.title: Bayes as a tree: which box was it?

steps.caption: Pick a box at random: 0.5 each. Box 1 has 3 white, 1 black. Box 2 has 1 white, 3 black.
Draw a ball from the chosen box. Box 1 gives white with 0.75. Box 2 gives white with 0.25.
Multiply along a path. Box 1 then white: 0.5 x 0.75 = 0.375.
Box 2 then white: 0.5 x 0.25 = 0.125.
We saw white, so the black paths did not happen. P(Box 1 | white) = 0.375 / (0.375 + 0.125) = 0.75.
Imagine 10,000 people. 1 in 200 is 50 sick, so 9,950 are healthy.
Sick people who test positive: 90% of 50 = 45.
Healthy people who test positive: 4% of 9,950 = 398.
All positives: 45 + 398 = 443.
Chance you are sick, given positive: 45 / 443, about 0.102.
A box holds a fair coin and a two-headed coin, equally likely. Prior: 0.5 each.
A toss shows heads. Multiply each by the chance of heads: fair 0.5, two-headed 1.
The bars no longer sum to 1. Divide by the total 0.75: the posterior is 1/3 and 2/3.
A second head. Multiply again: fair 1/3 x 0.5, two-headed 2/3 x 1.
Divide by the total 5/6 again. After two heads, the two-headed coin has probability 0.8.
The cases are M1 (probability 0.6) and M2 (probability 0.4). They add to 1.
Route through M1: 0.6 × 0.02 = 0.012.
Route through M2: 0.4 × 0.05 = 0.020.
Add the routes: P(defective) = 0.012 + 0.020 = 0.032.
Priors: P(M1) = 0.6 and P(M2) = 0.4.
Likelihood of 'defective': 0.02 under M1 and 0.05 under M2.
Multiply prior × likelihood. M1: 0.6 × 0.02 = 0.012. M2: 0.4 × 0.05 = 0.020.
Add them to get the evidence: P(defective) = 0.012 + 0.020 = 0.032.
Divide: P(M2 | defective) = 0.020 / 0.032 = 0.625.
